purpose: Lenacapavir is used to treat HIV-1 infection in adults whose HIV has not been controlled by other HIV medications. It is used along with other HIV medicines as part of a combination treatment plan. It is not a cure for HIV, but it helps lower the amount of virus in your body and keeps your immune system stronger.
how_it_works: HIV has a protein shell called a capsid that protects the virus and helps it multiply inside your body. Lenacapavir works by attaching to this capsid and blocking it at multiple steps, so the virus cannot make copies of itself. Think of it like jamming the gears of the virus so it cannot spread or grow.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include injection site reactions such as redness, swelling, or a lump under the skin where the shot was given. Some people may feel nausea or have elevated blood sugar levels. You might also notice a small bump under the skin at the injection site that can last for several months but is usually not harmful.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have liver problems, since lenacapavir is processed by the liver. This medication can interact with many other drugs, so always share a full list of your medications with your healthcare team. Do not stop taking your other HIV medicines without talking to your doctor first, as stopping can allow the virus to become resistant. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor.
typical_dosing: Lenacapavir is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection) by a healthcare provider. The usual schedule starts with injections on Day 1 and Day 2, then again on Day 8, and then once every 6 months after that. Because it is only given twice a year after the starting doses, it can be much more convenient than taking a daily pill.
